## 1. AI-assisted translation projects (2022–2026)

- **Roger Pearse (roger-pearse.com / tertullian.org).** One-man, ad hoc. Since 2024 he has run OCR'd medieval Greek, Latin and Arabic-Christian texts (Methodius ad Theodorum, a Life of Isidore of Pelusium, Eutychius, Aeneas of Gaza) through ChatGPT 3.5/4, Bard and DeepSeek, and posts drafts on his blog ([tag](https://www.roger-pearse.com/weblog/tag/ai-translation/)). There is no formal review. Best-known failure: asked to translate a Ge'ez homily, ChatGPT returned the Nicene Creed ([post](https://roger-pearse.com/weblog/2024/01/19/the-perils-of-ai-translation)). His conclusion: "you have to be able to check."
- **Bibliothecarius Modernus (Ryan Wolfslayer).** AI English versions of 225 Patrologia Latina texts, released under CC0. The 2024–25 editions had light checks. Since Sept 2026 the workflow adds a deterministic source-coverage check, review by a *different model family*, and per-segment provenance. The project calls the results "introductory guides rather than scholarly editions." There is no expert editor and no commentary ([GitHub](https://github.com/wryan14/Latin-Patristic-Texts), [site](https://bibliothecarius-modernus.github.io)). This is the closest existing analogue to Neoscholia, but it is Latin-only, popular in aim, and without an apparatus.
- **Sefaria.** Only 24% of its Hebrew texts have English translations. Its first AI-assisted full translation, *Kli Yakar* (Feb 2026), was drafted by Claude 3.7 and then reviewed word by word for six months by Francis Nataf, who estimates it saved 50–75% of the time ([Q&A](https://voices.sefaria.org/sheets/708436), [eJP](https://ejewishphilanthropy.com/?p=174283)). A separate independent effort translated the *Aruch HaShulchan* (3.4M words) with Gemini 3 Flash and graded a 100-sample with GPT-5.4: 29% good, 54% needing style fixes, 17% with errors. Code is open ([Seforim Blog](https://seforimblog.com/2026/05/translating-the-aruch-hashulchan-with-ai-method-and-lessons/)).
- **Perseus (Gregory Crane).** Uses LLMs (DeepSeek, Claude, Gemini) to add translations and glosses to the OGA treebank and to build aligned readers, rather than to publish standalone new translations ([Aug 2026](https://sites.tufts.edu/perseusupdates/2026/08/31/in-praise-of-the-open-digital-classics-ecosystem/); [CR 2025](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/classical-review/article/greek-latin-and-augmented-intelligence-the-other-ai/3B0154E88FBEAEC34B367C11F2A38BBA)).
- **CANOPOS (Macquarie, Greta Hawes).** A peer-reviewed mythography repository whose translations feed ToposText and Perseus. In 2026 it is producing a hybrid human-ML *first* English translation of Stephanus' *Ethnica* ([project](https://researchers.mq.edu.au/en/projects/canopos/)).
- **Evaluation research.**
  - Zainaldin et al. tested ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini on Galen ([arXiv 2602.24119](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.24119)). Mean MQM score was 95.2 on the already-translated *De temperamentis* but 79.9 on the never-translated *De compositione medicamentorum per genera*, with two catastrophic passages. How rare the terminology is predicted failure (r = −0.97).
  - A Pali study found that sending only the top 10% of passages by GEMBA risk score to human reviewers caught 81.6% of major errors ([arXiv 2609.14963](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14963)).
- **Cuneiform.**
  - Gutherz et al. 2023 trained a neural model on 8,056 ORACC texts and reached BLEU 37.47 (transliteration → English) and 36.52 (cuneiform → English). The authors document hallucinations and present the model as a tool for human–machine collaboration ([PNAS Nexus](https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/2/5/pgad096/7147349)).
  - The eBL Fragmentarium at LMU uses machine matching to join fragments. It was opened to the public in Feb 2023 and has added more than 100 lines to Gilgamesh ([LMU](https://www.lmu.de/en/newsroom/news-overview/news/electronic-babylonian-literature-playing-with-the-source-of-world-literature-4d9706d5.html)). It restores and joins texts rather than translating them; licence unknown.
- **Size of the gap.** Bebliotheca counts 2,316 Greek works, about 75% of them without an English translation ([post](https://thanosapollo.org/posts/patrologia-graeca-bebliotheca/)).

## 3. Russian-language landscape

- [ancientrome.ru](https://www.ancientrome.ru/antlitr/) is a catalogue of existing Russian translations; nothing on it is AI-produced.
- [vostlit.info](https://www.vostlit.info/) mostly reprints published translations; no licence stated.
- ΣΧΟΛΗ (Novosibirsk, Afonasin; [schole.ru](https://classics.nsu.ru/schole/1/schole-1-1.pdf)) and IOSPE3 publish commented Russian translations.
- I found **no Russian AI-assisted scholarly translation platform**. My web-search allowance ran out before I could do targeted Russian-language searches, so this "none" is provisional.

## 4. Name check: "Neoscholia"

- **Web:** no exact hits; only near-matches in biological names.
- **Domains:** RDAP returned 404 (not registered) for neoscholia.com, neoscholia.org and neoscholia.net on 2026-10-05. There is also no DNS record for neoscholia.ru, neoscholia.io or neo-scholia.org.
- **GitHub and PyPI:** 0 repositories; the username and package name are both free.
- **Not checked:** trademarks.
- **Similar names:**
  - ΣΧΟΛΗ/Schole (Novosibirsk journal; the closest Russian association)
  - *Scholia* (Natal/Otago classics journal)
  - Scholia (a Wikidata tool)
  - "Neo-scholastic" (Thomist philosophy, e.g. *Rivista di Filosofia Neo-Scolastica*), which is a real risk of confusion. A subtitle such as "New scholia on untranslated antiquity" would help.
- **Recommendation:** register .org, .com and .ru now.

## 5. Unoccupied niche

No project combines all of the following:
1. Classical and late-antique **secular** Greek and Latin: scholia, grammarians, paradoxographers, technical writers, the Alexander tradition. Patristic Latin and Hebrew are already taken by AI projects.
2. **Russian as a primary target**, with parallel English.
3. A **published multi-model adversarial review log** as part of the apparatus, together with sign-off by a named human expert.
4. A critical commentary.
5. Per-segment provenance (model, version, prompt, date), versioning and DOIs.

Bibliothecarius Modernus covers (5) and part of (3). SOL and ACA cover (3) and (4) but use human labour. Sefaria and CANOPOS have human review but use AI only as a drafter, and do not show the review to readers.

## 6. Lessons learned

- **Failure is predictable.** Rare terminology and dense technical prose drive it (Galen study). Build glossaries for each text, and send passages with rare lemmas to the expert by default.
- **Corrupt or obscure input makes models invent plausible text** (Pearse). Run segment-level checks that every part of the source is covered, align translation to source, and clean the OCR first.
- **Model-on-model review reduces errors but does not remove them.** About 17% of the Aruch HaShulchan sample still had errors. Use risk triage (GEMBA, disagreement between models' translations) to decide where human time goes.
- **Borrow the SOL and ACA model:** visible vetting levels (AI draft → cross-reviewed → expert-vetted) and an audit trail for each unit.
- **Licensing:**
  - An NC licence will not mix with First1KGreek's CC BY-SA. License the source text and the translation separately.
  - NC also limits reuse by Perseus and ToposText.
  - Some recent critical editions are protected (e.g. German §70 UrhG; from my own knowledge, not verified in this research), so prefer pre-1950 or openly licensed texts.

## 7. Potential partners

- Perseus/OGL (Crane) and First1KGreek, for source texts and display.
- The CGPG Patrologia Graeca team (UCLouvain).
- CANOPOS (Hawes) and the Zainaldin/Schiefsky group, for evaluation method.
- Suda On Line, for scholia and lexica.
- IOSPE3 (Ivantchik) and ΣΧΟΛΗ (Afonasin), for Russian.
- ToposText (Kiesling), for distribution.
- Roger Pearse and Bibliothecarius Modernus, to compare pipelines.

# Neoscholia: legal & licensing landscape (research summary, not legal advice)

## (a) Rights in critical editions
- **EU framework.** Under Term Directive 2006/116/EC, member states *may* protect "critical and scientific publications" of public-domain (PD) works for at most 30 years (art. 5). They *must* give 25 years of protection to whoever first publishes a previously unpublished PD work (art. 4). Art. 4 matters for editiones principes of papyri and manuscripts ([text](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2006/116/body/adopted)).
- **Germany:** §70 UrhG protects editions that result from "wissenschaftlich sichtender Tätigkeit" and differ substantially from earlier editions, for 25 years from appearance. §71 gives 25 years for a first publication ([§70](https://lexetius.com/UrhG/70), [§71](https://lexetius.com/UrhG/71)).
- **Italy:** art. 85-quater L. 633/1941 gives 20 years from first publication, plus the curator's right to be named ([filodiritto](https://www.filodiritto.com/codici/legge-sulla-protezione-del-diritto-dautore-protezione-del-diritto-dautore-e-di-altri-diritti-connessi-al-suo-esercizio-l-22-aprile-1941-n-633/capo-iii-ter-diritti-relativi-ad-edizioni-critiche-e-scientifiche-di-opere-di-pubblico-dominio/art-85-0)). I did not verify other member states (e.g. Spain).
- **New EU-wide layer (major uncertainty):** CJEU C-649/23 *Institutul G. Călinescu* (19 Mar 2026).
  - A critical edition that restores a PD text with comments and apparatus may be a full copyright *work* if it reflects the editor's "free and creative choices".
  - Purely technical choices (grammatical, lexical) are not enough, and the PD text itself does not become private property again ([ipcuria](https://ipcuria.eu/case?reference=C-649%2F23), [IPKat](https://ipkitten.blogspot.com/2026/03/cjeu-rules-that-derivative-works-enjoy.html), [Kluwer](https://legalblogs.wolterskluwer.com/copyright-blog/reconstructing-the-author-not-re-privatising-the-text-the-eu-concept-of-work-after-institutul-g-calinescu/)).
  - Consequence: the apparatus, prefaces and possibly the arrangement of 20th-c. editions can be protected for the editor's life + 70 years, well beyond the 20/25-year related rights.
- **UK:** there is no edition right, but the typographical arrangement of a published edition is protected for 25 years (CDPA s.15, [legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1988/48/section/15)). *Sawkins v Hyperion* held a scholarly edition of PD music to be original ([judgment](https://caselaw.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ewhc/ch/2004/1530)).
- **US:**
  - *Feist* (1991) requires independent creation plus a "modicum of creativity"; facts are not protected ([LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/499/340)).
  - There is no database right and no edition right. Emendations that aim to recover the author's words are arguably unprotectable facts; prose commentary is protected.
  - I found no controlling US case. By contrast, Israel's *Qimron v. Shanks* (2000) protected a reconstructed Qumran text ([summary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qimron_v._Shanks)).
  - Works published in 1930 or earlier are in the US public domain ([Duke](https://web.law.duke.edu/cspd/publicdomainday/2026/)).
- **Russia:** there is no §70 analogue.
  - The publisher right (ст. 1337–1344 ГК РФ) covers only *previously unpublished* PD works published after 31.12.2007. It lasts 25 years from 1 January of the year after publication ([ст. 1337](https://legalacts.ru/kodeks/GK-RF-chast-4/razdel-vii/glava-71/ss-6/statja-1337/), [ст. 1340](https://gkodeksrf.ru/ch-4/rzd-7/gl-71/prg-6/st-1340-gk-rf)).
  - Translations and other derivative or composite works are protected (ст. 1260, [text](https://www.zakonrf.info/gk/1260/)), so a creative edition may qualify.

## (b) Digital corpora
- **Closed corpora — use for checking only, never as the published source:**
  - **TLG:** copyrighted; no downloading, copying or redistribution ([terms](https://stephanus.tlg.uci.edu/copyright.php)).
  - **Brepols LLT:** only insubstantial non-commercial extraction is allowed, and no derived databases ([terms PDF](https://www.uni-erfurt.de/fileadmin/einrichtung/bibliothek/Themen/Lizenzen/Brepols_Nutzungsbedingungen.pdf)). In the EU the 15-year database right also applies ([Dir. 96/9](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/1996/9)).
  - **PHI Latin:** personal study only ([site](https://latin.packhum.org/)).
- **Openly licensed corpora:**
  - **Perseus canonical-greekLit and OGL First1KGreek:** CC BY-SA 4.0 ([Perseus](https://github.com/PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit), [OGL](https://github.com/OpenGreekAndLatin/First1KGreek)).
  - **papyri.info** (DDbDP/HGV/APIS): CC BY 3.0 ([idp.data](https://github.com/papyri/idp.data)).
  - **Corpus Corporum:** CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 according to a 2021 readme ([Uppsala](https://sprakbanken-clarin.lingfil.uu.se/histcorp/readme/latin-readme-corporum)); check each text.
- **Migne PG/PL** are PD; scans are on [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/Patrologia_Graeca_vol_003). **HathiTrust** restricts re-hosting of Google-digitized scans, but not text transcribed or translated from them ([HathiTrust](https://hathitrust.atlassian.net/wiki/x/gYBAjg)).
- **Licence conflict:**
  - Adaptations of BY-SA material may only be licensed BY-SA 4.0 or later, FAL 1.3 or GPLv3 ([CC](https://creativecommons.org/share-your-work/licensing-considerations/compatible-licenses/)). So any OGL/Perseus text you republish must stay BY-SA, not NC.
  - It is doubtful, but untested, that a translation made from a BY-SA digitisation of a PD work counts as "Adapted Material". The licence covers only "Copyright and Similar Rights" ([legalcode](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/legalcode.en)).

## (c) Copyrightability of AI output
- **US:**
  - The Copyright Office's Part 2 report (29 Jan 2025) concludes:
    - purely AI-generated material is unprotected;
    - prompts alone are not enough;
    - human expressive inputs, creative selection or arrangement, and creative modifications are protected ([report](https://www.copyright.gov/ai/Copyright-and-Artificial-Intelligence-Part-2-Copyrightability-Report.pdf)).
  - Registrations must disclose AI-generated material ([2023 guidance](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2023-03-16/pdf/2023-05321.pdf)).
  - In *Thaler*, the D.C. Circuit ruled on 18 Mar 2025 that an author must be human; the Supreme Court denied certiorari on 2 Mar 2026 ([Baker Donelson](https://www.bakerdonelson.com/supreme-court-denies-certiorari-in-thaler-v-perlmutter-ai-cannot-be-an-author-under-the-copyright-act)).
  - An AI translation of a PD text contains no expressive input of your own, so the raw output is likely PD.
- **EU:**
  - Originality requires human free and creative choices.
  - The Prague Municipal Court denied protection to an AI-generated image ([Merlin](https://merlin.obs.coe.int/article/10047)).
  - The European Parliament resolution of 10 Mar 2026 says fully AI-generated content "should remain ineligible" ([Merlin](https://merlin.obs.coe.int/article/10499)).
- **Russia:**
  - An author is a "гражданин, творческим трудом которого создан" the result (ст. 1228, [text](https://www.zakonrf.info/gk/1228/)).
  - The Moscow Arbitrazh Court (А40-200471/2023) treated deepfake technology as a tool where humans made the creative contribution ([pravo.ru](https://pravo.ru/news/251448/)).
- **What this means for the licence:** CC BY-NC(-SA) binds only the protected layers: human revisions, human commentary, selection and arrangement, and the EU database right. Raw AI drafts and AI reviews can probably be reused commercially by anyone. Documented human editing is both the legal hook and the scholarly warrant.

## (d) "Open source" vs non-commercial
- OSD criterion 6 forbids restrictions on fields of endeavour, including commercial use ([OSI](https://opensource.org/osd-annotated)).
- The Open Definition lists NC licences as non-conformant ([OD](https://opendefinition.org/licenses/nonconformant/)).
- Only BY and BY-SA are "Approved for Free Cultural Works" ([CC](https://creativecommons.org/public-domain/freeworks/)), so NC content cannot go into Wikipedia or Wikisource.
- Describe the platform as "open access, non-commercial", not "open source".

## (e) Provider terms
- **OpenAI:** assigns output rights "if any" and forbids representing output as human-generated ([terms](https://openai.com/policies/row-terms-of-use/)). Its publication policy asks for clear disclosure of the AI's role ([policy](https://openai.com/policies/sharing-publication-policy)). Both pages returned 403, so this comes from search results; verify.
- **Anthropic:** assigns rights "(if any)" in Outputs and bans using them to train competing models ([consumer](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/consumer-terms), [commercial](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/commercial-terms)).
- **Google Gemini API:** Google "won't claim ownership" but may generate similar content for others. Using the service to develop competing models is banned. Clients serving EEA/UK/CH users may use Paid Services only ([terms](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms)).
- None of the three bars publishing or CC-licensing outputs, and none warrants that outputs are copyrightable. The risk area is fine-tuning your own model on these outputs.
- **EU AI Act art. 50(4)** (from 2 Aug 2026): AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must be labelled, unless it was human-reviewed under someone's editorial responsibility ([guide](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/transparency-rules-article-50/)). I could not verify any changes from the Digital Omnibus.

## Recommendations
1. **Use layered, machine-readable licences** (in the TEI header or as SPDX identifiers):
   - **Source text:** re-transcribed from PD editions under the Public Domain Mark, or taken from OGL/Perseus under CC BY-SA with attribution. Never take text from TLG, LLT or PHI.
   - **Human-edited translation and commentary:** CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, with a notice that AI-generated portions may be unprotected. Choose CC BY-SA instead if reuse on Wikisource matters more than the NC restriction.
   - **Raw AI drafts and review logs:** CC0.
   - **Code:** AGPL-3.0 or Apache-2.0. Code under an NC licence is not open source.
2. **When the best edition is recent:** translate, cite its readings and quote sparingly, but do not reproduce its text or apparatus. Otherwise ask the editor or publisher for permission.
3. **Keep provenance:** model and version, prompts, git diffs of every human edit, a named editor with ORCID, and a DOI via Zenodo.
4. **Disclose AI's role:** put an AI-role statement on every text.
5. **Get legal review:** choose the hosting jurisdiction deliberately and have Russian and EU IP counsel review the setup, especially exposure under Călinescu.

**Open uncertainties:** the scope of Călinescu; whether NC can be enforced on AI-heavy text; how far ShareAlike reaches; Russian practice on AI authorship; AI Act timing.

key_facts.fact: Germany §70 UrhG protects scholarly editions of unprotected texts (result of 'wissenschaftlich sichtender Tätigkeit', substantially different from earlier editions) for 25 years from appearance; the right belongs to the editor.
Italy art. 85-quater L. 633/1941 grants exclusive economic rights in critical and scientific editions of PD works for 20 years from first lawful publication.

Term Directive 2006/116/EC: art. 5 lets member states protect critical/scientific publications of PD works for max. 30 years (optional); art. 4 mandates 25 years for whoever first publishes a previously unpublished PD work.

CJEU C-649/23 Institutul G. Călinescu (19 Mar 2026): a critical edition restoring a PD text with comments and apparatus may be a copyright-protected work if it reflects the editor's free and creative choices and is identifiable with sufficient precision.

Russian publisher right (ст. 1337–1344 ГК РФ) applies only to previously unpublished PD works published after 31.12.2007 and lasts 25 years from 1 January of the year after publication; there is no general related right for critical editions.
Under ст. 1228 ГК РФ only a citizen whose creative labour produced the result can be an author; under ст. 1260 a translator holds copyright in the translation (derivative work).

US Copyright Office Part 2 report (29 Jan 2025): purely AI-generated material is not protected; prompts alone give insufficient control; human expressive inputs, creative selection/arrangement and creative modifications of AI output are protectable.
Thaler v. Perlmutter: the D.C. Circuit held on 18 Mar 2025 that the Copyright Act requires a human author; the Supreme Court denied certiorari on 2 Mar 2026 (No. 25-449).
European Parliament resolution of 10 Mar 2026 (2025/2058(INI)) states that content fully generated by AI that does not meet copyright criteria should remain ineligible for protection.
TLG materials are copyrighted by the Regents of the University of California; downloading, copying and redistribution are prohibited, so TLG text cannot serve as the published source text.
Perseus canonical-greekLit and OGL First1KGreek are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; papyri.info data (idp.data: DDbDP, HGV, APIS) is CC BY 3.0.
Adaptations of CC BY-SA 4.0 material may only be licensed under BY-SA 4.0 or later, Free Art License 1.3 or GPLv3 (one-way), so OGL/Perseus-derived source layers cannot be relicensed NC.

The Open Definition treats CC NonCommercial licences as non-conformant (they discriminate against fields of endeavour), and OSD criterion 6 forbids commercial-use restrictions, so an NC project is 'open access', not 'open source/open'.

Anthropic assigns users its right, title and interest (if any) in Outputs and bars using them to train competing models; the Gemini API terms say Google won't claim ownership of generated content but bar developing competing models; OpenAI assigns output rights and bars representing output as human-generated.

EU AI Act art. 50(4) (applicable from 2 Aug 2026) requires disclosure of AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless it underwent human review/editorial control under someone's editorial responsibility; possible Digital Omnibus changes were not verified.

## 1. Evidence base, 2023–2026

**Ancient Greek.** The key study is Zainaldin et al. 2026. Domain experts used MQM to score claude-sonnet-4.5, gpt-5 and gemini-2.5-pro on Galen (https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.24119). The score was 95.2/100 on the already-translated *De temperamentis* but only 79.9 on the never fully translated *De compositione medicamentorum per genera*. Under the strict scheme (no critical errors allowed), 87% of passages passed for the first text and 43% for the second. Density of rare terms, measured by Diorisis frequency, predicted the failures (r≈−.97). Every passage with a rare-term ratio above .30 failed catastrophically in all three models (GPT-5 scored 0 on one). Errors clustered on minerals, plants and drug properties, including terms with clear English equivalents. Models also "confidently render nonsense" when the text is corrupt.

Wannaz & Miyagawa (NLP4DH 2024, https://aclanthology.org/2024.nlp4dh-1.44/) tested 9 LLMs on ostraca. Claude 3 Opus and GPT-4o led for Greek, and hallucination was "markedly more common" for Coptic. Ströbel & Maier (CHR 2025, https://anthology.ach.org/volumes/vol0003/echoes-of-antiquity-towards-understanding/) found that LLM translations fall back on frequent patterns and lose interpretive range, especially in poetry. Their lab also found that ChatGPT reproduced Fowler's 1914 *Apology* word for word (https://www.hist.uzh.ch/de/fachbereiche/altegeschichte/lehrstuehle/maier/AIncient-Studies-Lab/Projects/Building-a-Comparative-Translation-Database-for-Classical-Texts-with-LLMs.html).

**Latin.** Volk et al. (LT4HALA 2024, https://aclanthology.org/2024.lt4hala-1.15/) found GPT-4 "clearly superior" to earlier systems on 16th-c. letters. Torres Aguilar (https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01454) showed that base LLMs simplify passives, case government and pronoun scope. A pipeline with an NLLB draft, retrieval of similar passages and Llama-3.3-70B refinement matched GPT-5 (COMET ≈0.75).

**Other languages.**
- **Akkadian:** a neural MT model reached BLEU ≈37 but produced fluent hallucinations and works best on short sentences (Gutherz et al. 2023, https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/2/5/pgad096/7147349). The EvaCun shared task (ALP 2025, https://aclweb.org/portal/node/5996) covered lemmatization and token restoration, not translation.
- **Syriac/Armenian/Georgian:** few-shot GPT-4 lemmatization and POS tagging are competitive (https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15753). I found no serious evaluation of LLM translation of Syriac.
- **Classical Arabic:** the ATHAR dataset (66k pairs, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.19835) was built because current LLMs show gaps.
- **Byzantine Greek:** I found no dedicated evaluation of LLM translation. Logion detects scribal errors in Psellos (https://classics.princeton.edu/research/bookshelf/artificial-intelligence-and-greek-philology-experiment).

**Lacunae.** Specialist models help when a human interprets the output. With Ithaca, historians' restoration accuracy rose from 25% to 72% (https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/predicting-the-past-with-ithaca/). Aeneas reaches 73% top-20 accuracy on gaps of up to 10 characters but is weak on names and numbers (https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/aeneas-transforms-how-historians-connect-the-past/).

**Russian.** I found no published evaluation of LLM translation from an ancient language into Russian (searched in English and Russian). Indirect evidence:
- In WMT24 human evaluation of En→Ru, the human reference scored 89.2, Claude-3.5 88.2 and GPT-4 85.0. A DFKI test suite there found Claude weak on function words and GPT-4 worse than several NMT systems into Russian (https://aclanthology.org/2024.wmt-1.1.pdf).
- Llama models' internal "concept space" sits closer to English (https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.820).
- There is far more Greek/Latin–English parallel text (Loeb, Perseus) than Greek/Latin–Russian.

Expect English calques, inconsistent transliteration and weaker terminology in Russian. Measure this; do not assume either way.

## 2. Failure modes
1. Fluent hallucination on rare vocabulary.
2. Smoothing corrupt text or lacunae into plausible sense.
3. Omissions: Bibliothecarius Modernus's CC0 translations of the Patrologia Latina recorded 12 editions with missing Latin passages; its legacy corpus is unreviewed (https://github.com/wryan14/Latin-Patristic-Texts).
4. Reproducing existing translations from memory.
5. Simplified syntax.
6. Fabricated references: in a 2023 test, 18% of GPT-4's citations did not exist (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10484980/).
7. Homogenized style.
8. Misidentified quotations: no benchmark found, so treat as high-risk.

## 3. Grounding
- **Dictionary entries in the prompt:** this lifted ChatGPT's En→Serbian score from 3.08 to 42.63 chrF++ (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.06575). Inject entries per lemma from LSJ, Lampe, LBG (TLG, registration required), Lewis & Short and Dvoretsky.
- **Morphology:** odyCy (MIT licence, state of the art on UD Perseus; https://github.com/centre-for-humanities-computing/odyCy), GreTa/PhilTa (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13698), Morpheus and CLTK. Use Diorisis frequencies to sort passages by risk.
- **Source hygiene:** OCR of the Patrologia Graeca reaches WER 4.69% (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.09470), roughly one wrong word in 20. Collate the text before translating.

## 4. Multi-agent and LLM-judge evidence
**Positive:**
- Human readers preferred TransAgents' multi-agent literary translations even though they scored lower on d-BLEU (https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.11804).
- Multi-agent debate improves LLM evaluation of MT (M-MAD, https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.20127).

**Caveats:**
- Multi-agent debate often fails to beat simple single-model baselines; using different models is what helps (https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08788).
- In En→Ja translation, gains come early; later rounds over-revise and the meaning drifts (EAMT 2026, https://aclanthology.org/2026.eamt-1.16/).
- A model correcting itself without outside feedback can make things worse (https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798).

**Judge biases:**
- Models prefer their own output (https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13076).
- Self-refinement amplifies that bias, including in translation (https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.826).
- Judges are biased by answer position and length (https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685).
- A panel of diverse judge models reduces single-model bias (https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.18796).
- Automatic metrics hide disasters: COMET turned a 56.7-point drop in the human score into a 4.8% dip (Galen study).

## 5. Recommended pipeline
0. **Source:** use a public-domain critical text collated against print. Split it into segments with CTS URNs. Encode lacunae, cruces and supplements as protected tokens and keep the apparatus.
1. **Automatic pre-analysis:** lemmatize and parse; compute each passage's rare-term ratio; build lexicon packets; retrieve parallels from TLG, Perseus and PHI; flag passages with a ratio above .30.
2. **Translate:** produce at least 3 independent drafts from different model families plus one open-weight model. Translate directly into English and into Russian, never Russian via English. Give a literal layer and a readable layer, with required uncertainty tags. Unresolved terms are transliterated and flagged.
3. **Annotate:** write the commentary as atomic claims, each tied to a passage of the text or to a reference that can be checked.
4. **Cross-review:** only other model families review a draft, blind and in random order, controlling for length. Reviewers mark MQM error spans: terminology, mistranslation, addition, omission, over- and under-translation, each with a severity. Allow at most 2 rounds, and freeze segments that pass without major errors.
5. **Adjudicate:** a separate model picks or merges per segment and logs its rationale and any dissent. Anything still unresolved goes to a human.
6. **Human sign-off:** the editor reviews every flagged segment plus a random 15% of unflagged ones. A Russian-native classicist reviews the Russian version.
7. **Publish:** release model IDs, prompts, review logs and diffs, with status labels, a versioned DOI and open errata.

## 6. Quality gates before publication
- **G1 Coverage:** 100% of segments aligned, with outlier length ratios checked.
- **G2 Lacunae:** no unmarked supplements; every lacuna and crux is mirrored in the translation.
- **G3 Errors:** no unresolved critical MQM errors; the audited sample scores at least 95; the strict pass rate is published.
- **G4 Rare terms:** each rare term carries a lexicon citation or a flagged transliteration; the glossary is consistent between English and Russian.
- **G5 References:** 100% of citations resolve; every ancient passage cited resolves and its quotation matches the text.
- **G6 Transparency:** cross-model disagreement and the residual error rate from the random audit are published.
- **G7 Copying:** word-sequence overlap with any existing translation stays below a set threshold.
- **G8 Metrics:** COMET and BERTScore are used only to sort passages, never to approve them.
- **G9 Sign-off:** a named human editor signs each release.

Strict pass rates (no critical errors) were 87% vs 43%.

In the Galen study, density of rare terms (by Diorisis frequency) predicted quality (r≈−.97). The UZH AIncient Studies Lab found that ChatGPT reproduced Fowler's 1914 translation of Plato's Apology word for word. LLMs can regurgitate existing translations instead of translating independently.

Llama-2 models process concepts in an internal space closer to English than to the input language. This suggests a risk of English-pivot calques when translating into Russian (an inference, not measured for ancient languages).
Putting dictionary entries in the prompt (Chain-of-Dictionary) raised ChatGPT's En→Serbian (Cyrillic) score from 3.08 to 42.63 chrF++. Lexicon grounding strongly helps with rare words.

Bibliothecarius Modernus publishes CC0 AI translations of about 225 Patrologia Latina texts as introductory guides. Its 2024–25 legacy corpus is unreviewed and 12 editions recorded missing Latin passages; newer editions add source-coverage checks and review by different model families.

## Scale of untranslated ancient literature: what can actually be quantified

**Bottom line.** Nobody has published a census of how much ancient Greek or Latin has an English translation, and I found none for Russian either. The numbers that do exist are partial: corpus sizes, rates for particular sub-corpora, and scholars' estimates. Together they show a clear gradient. The classical canon up to about 300 CE is almost fully translated into English and largely into Russian. The untranslated mass sits in late antique, technical, exegetical and scholiastic Greek, in Byzantine texts, and in post-classical Latin, and above all in documentary material (cuneiform, papyri). Claims that a given text is "untranslated" often turn out to be wrong (see the Russian case of Libanius below), so each one has to be checked individually.

### 1. Greek: size of the corpus
- **TLG today:** "more than 125 million words from over 12,000 works associated with 4,000 authors", from Homer to 1453 plus post-Byzantine texts ([TLG](https://stephanus.tlg.uci.edu/tlg.php)). Wikipedia gives about 110 million Greek words, 1.6 million wordforms and 250,000 lemmata ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thesaurus_Linguae_Graecae)).
- **Antiquity alone:** TLG version E, which has all texts to 600 CE plus a Byzantine selection, had about 76 million words. Peust (2000) uses 57 million words as the Greek corpus to 300 CE and Latin at about 10 million (Thesaurus Linguae Latinae slips). So Greek to 300 CE is roughly 5–6 times larger than Latin ([Wikipedia, "Ancient text corpora", citing Peust, *Lingua Aegyptia* 7, 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_text_corpora)).
- **Byzantine portion:** about 125 million minus about 76 million leaves roughly 50 million or more words after 600 CE, and that is only what TLG holds. This is my own arithmetic (medium confidence).
- **Digitization is still incomplete:** about 6 million tokens from the volumes of Migne's Patrologia Graeca that had never been digitized were OCR'd and released only in 2026 ([Vidal-Gorène & Kindt, arXiv 2603.09470](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.09470)).

### 2. Greek: translated share (only proxies exist)
- **Byzantine science and philosophy:** Mavroudi estimates "less than 5 percent" of the surviving production has even been *published*, which means far less has been translated (*Speculum* 90, 2015, p. 38; quoted by [Roger Pearse](https://www.roger-pearse.com/weblog/2017/09/08/less-than-5-of-byzantine-scientific-texts-have-been-published/)).
- **Galen:** his works make up about 10% of all Greek literature down to 350 CE ([Zainaldin et al., arXiv 2602.24119](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2602.24119.md)). In 1999 "two-thirds of the corpus still awaits an English translation" ([*New Surveys in the Classics* 29](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/new-surveys-in-the-classics/article/epilogue/F843155AD123D711C247191BCA7968B5)). That gap has narrowed since then through the Cambridge and Loeb Galen volumes. By my inference, Galen alone accounted for about 6–7% of pre-350 Greek words lacking English in 1999.
- **Aristotle commentators:** the Commentaria in Aristotelem Graeca runs to 23 volumes. The Ancient Commentators project has published "over 100 volumes… usually for the first time" in English ([ACA](https://www.ancientcommentators.org.uk/)). For English this gap is mostly closed. Russian status unknown.
- **Suda:** all 31,000+ entries were translated into English by more than 200 volunteers (1998–2014), under a CC BY-NC-SA licence ([SOL](https://www.cs.uky.edu/~raphael/sol/sol-html/)). This is the closest precedent to Neoscholia's model.
- **Early-modern printed Greek:** of 8,509 distinct "ancient Greek" works printed 1450–1700 (Universal Short Title Catalogue), only 1.55% match an English translation. This counts printed titles, not the ancient corpus, so read it with caution ([Source Library, May 2026](https://sourcelibrary.org/research/translation-gap)).
- **Patristics:** I could only find guesses on forums ("60–70%" or "80%" untranslated into English). Unverified, low confidence.

### 3. Latin
- **Classical:** about 10 million words to 300 CE (Peust, above), essentially all translated into English.
- **Late antique to modern:** the Library of Latin Texts (Series A) held more than 83 million words in 4,124 works as of 2018 ([Brepols](https://about.brepolis.net/library-of-latin-texts-series-a/)). The Patrologia Latina runs to 221 volumes; English patristic series cover a small fraction (forum estimate, low confidence).
- **Early modern:** the Universal Short Title Catalogue lists 444,120 distinct Latin works printed 1450–1700, of which about 2–2.3% (about 8,644) have an English translation, with a ceiling of 3.8% under the loosest matching ([Source Library](https://sourcelibrary.org/research/translation-gap)). An earlier version of the same study gave 362,000 works and about 1–3% ([source](https://sourcelibrary.org/blog/untranslated-renaissance)).

### 4. Documentary corpora
- **Cuneiform:** more than 550,000 objects exist and more than 400,000 are catalogued ([York 2026](https://www.york.ac.uk/archaeology/about/news/2026/towards-universal-access-to-cuneiform-heritage/); [CDLI](https://cdli.earth/about)).
- **CDLI's own data:** the September 2024 newsletter lists 368,735 records, 151,024 with transliterations (41%) and **5,568 with translations (about 1.5%)** ([CDLI](https://cdli.earth/postings/218)). This counts only translations held inside CDLI; ORACC and print publications have more.
- **Published cuneiform:** about 144,000 Akkadian texts (9.9 million words) and 102,300 Sumerian texts (3.08 million words) (Streck, *MDOG* 142, 2010, via [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_text_corpora)).
- **Overall:** "most of these documents remain untranslated" ([Gordin et al., *PNAS Nexus* 2023](https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/2/5/pgad096/7147349)). Popular sources often quote "90% untranslated"; that figure is weakly sourced.
- **Oxyrhynchus papyri:** 5,476 items published (vol. 84, 2019) against an estimated 400,000 to more than 1 million fragments, i.e. about 0.5–1.4% ([Nongbri](https://brentnongbri.com/2019/10/20/how-much-material-from-oxyrhynchus-remains-unpublished/)).

### 5. Russian
- No census exists. The ancientrome.ru electronic library ([index](https://ancientrome.ru/antlitr/)) lists **159** author and collection entries (my count of its index). That is a floor for what is online in Russian, not a bibliography.
- **Coverage is uneven:**
  - **Galen:** Russian Wikipedia says only "two translations" exist (1971; a 2014 volume with three treatises), although the same page also lists a separate *De naturalibus facultatibus*. The near-absence of Galen alone means about 9% of pre-350 CE Greek has no Russian version (my inference) ([ru.wikipedia](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Гален)).
  - **Libanius:** the opposite case. All of his orations exist in Russian (Shestakov, Kazan 1912–16; reprinted St Petersburg 2014), plus Shabaga's version of Orations 19–23 in *Aristeas* 11 (2015) ([ru.wikipedia](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Либаний)). Older Russian translations from before 1917, in Kazan academic and church-academy editions, are a frequent trap when judging what is "untranslated".

### 6. Existing lists of untranslated texts
- Roger Pearse, "[Translations that ought to exist](https://www.roger-pearse.com/weblog/2009/02/16/translations-that-ought-to-exist/)" (2009). It names 15 texts, for example Cyril of Alexandria's *Contra Julianum* (about 100,000 words) and Eusebius' *Commentary on Psalms*. Several have since been translated. Pearse's ["Additional Texts"](https://ccel.org/ccel/pearse/morefathers/files/index.htm) collection gathers translations missing from the 19th-century English series of the Church Fathers (Ante-Nicene and Nicene/Post-Nicene Fathers).
- Princeton's [Modern Language Translations of Byzantine Sources](https://dpul.princeton.edu/greek-collections/about/princeton-byzantine-studies-databases) (Airtable database, maintained by D. Jenkins) is the best tool for checking whether a Byzantine text has a translation.
- I found no maintained Wikipedia or AWOL list of untranslated texts.

### Implications for Neoscholia
1. The untranslated Greek and Latin corpus is tens of millions of words at least. It is concentrated in:
   - Byzantine texts (about 50 million words or more in TLG; less than 5% of science and philosophy even edited);
   - Galen and other technical writers;
   - scholia, lexica and commentaries;
   - patristic exegesis;
   - late and Neo-Latin.
2. For Russian the gap is wider than for English. Texts with English but no Russian (the Aristotle commentators, most of Galen, Suda-type reference works) form a large, well-edited pool that qualifies under the first priority.
3. Suggested census method: TLG Canon entries × (Princeton database + Loeb/Budé/Ancient Commentators/Translated Texts for Historians + Russian Wikipedia sections on translations + ancientrome/simposium + the *Вестник древней истории* (ВДИ) and *Aristeas* indexes). Score each work as full, partial or no translation. No one has done this yet, and it would itself be a publishable dataset.

**Method note.** Status claims come from fetched pages: ru.wikipedia translation sections, ancientrome.ru, azbyka.ru and ΣΧΟΛΗ. The WebSearch budget ran out partway through. So "none" often means only "no translation listed in the ru.wiki article", which is moderate evidence. English status marked † is from memory and was not re-checked in this pass.

## 1. How to verify a Russian translation (workflow)
1. **ru.wikipedia author pages** ("Переводы/Сочинения" sections). These are the most systematic source, and some state gaps outright. For Choricius the article says no complete translation of any of his works exists (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Хорикий_Газский). Stub articles are weak evidence.
2. **ancientrome.ru, "Античная литература"** author catalogue with translated texts (https://ancientrome.ru/antlitr/index.htm). Example: Cassiodorus *Variae* books I–II, translated by С.В. Кулаев (https://ancientrome.ru/antlitr/cassiodorus/index.htm). Some pages are in windows-1251 and break scrapers.
3. **azbyka.ru/otechnik** for patristic and Byzantine texts. It exposes partial translations: Photius' *Myriobiblon* has only about 100 of roughly 280 codices (https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Fotij_Konstantinopolskij/biblioteka_miriobiblion/), and Eusebius' *Praeparatio* has only book XI (https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Evsevij_Kesarijskij/).
4. **eLibrary/CyberLeninka.** Many translations exist only as journal installments: ΣΧΟΛΗ, Аристей, ВДИ, Philologia Classica, Классическая и византийская традиция, Hypothekai.
5. **Soviet anthologies.** They are the main reason many authors count as "partial": *Поздняя греческая проза* (1960); *Памятники позднего античного ораторского и эпистолярного искусства* (1964); *Памятники поздней античной поэзии и прозы* (1964); *Памятники византийской литературы IV–IX вв.* (1968). ВДИ also printed Scythia/Caucasus excerpts (1947–49).
6. **РНБ/РГБ catalogues and bibliographies** (Свиясов 1998 for poetry; Любжин on Roman literature in Russia). These were not re-verified.

## 2. Series, institutions, theological academies
- **Литературные памятники**: since 1948, Наука/Ладомир, still active (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Литературные_памятники).
- **Памятники письменности Востока**: since 1959, about 257 volumes, active. It includes late-antique Manichaean and Pahlavi texts (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Памятники_письменности_Востока).
- **Греко-латинский кабинет Ю.А. Шичалина**: since 1990, active, publishes bilingual commented editions (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Греко-латинский_кабинет_Ю._А._Шичалина).
- **Theological academies, 19th–early 20th c.**
  - The СПбДА journal *Христианское чтение* ran 1821–1918, was revived in 1991, and joined the RSCI core in 2025 (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Христианское_чтение).
  - The Kazan circle produced Origen *De principiis* (Петров 1899) and *Contra Celsum* (Писарев 1912) (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ориген), and Libanius' *Речи* (Шестаков 1912/1916, 2 vols; new edition from 2014) (https://ru.wikisource.org/wiki/Автор:Либаний).
  - Net effect: the core Fathers exist in Russian, often reprinted on azbyka. Left out were marginal or condemned exegetes (Didymus, Theodore), Eusebius' apologetic encyclopaedias, and secular late-antique prose.
- **Active first-translation pipelines**
  - **ΣΧΟΛΗ** (Afonasin; open access, CC BY; Scopus/WoS/DOAJ; https://classics.nsu.ru/schole/). It is serializing Proclus' *In Timaeum* book II (Месяц, RSF 25-18-00141, 2026; https://classics.nsu.ru/schole/assets/files/20-2-mesyats.pdf).
  - **Belgorod circle** (Н.Н. Болгов): Priscian's *Panegyric*, Corippus' *In laudem Iustini*, Choricius.
  - **Individual translators:** М.М. Синица (John Lydus, partial, ongoing; https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Иоанн_Лид); С.И. Межерицкая (Aelius Aristides 2006–2020); Р.Л. Шмараков (Claudian complete 2008, Prudentius 2012); И.Ю. Шабага (*Panegyrici Latini* complete 2016); Ю.А. Шахова (Martianus complete 2019); Е.В. Старшова (Corippus *Iohannis* complete 2023); А.П. Большаков (Quintus complete 2016).
- **Lesson:** Late Latin poetry and panegyric are now largely covered. The untranslated mass is Greek commentary, rhetorical, technical and lexicographic prose, plus Byzantine scholarship.

## 3. Ranked gaps (RU status → EN)
1. **Stobaeus, *Anthologium*.** No complete translation in any modern language (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Стобей). The Wachsmuth–Hense text is public domain. Unique value as a source of fragments.
2. **Scholia** (Homer, Pindar, Aristophanes, Euripides). Russian: none. ru.wiki says scholia are "usually not translated" (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Схолии). English: partial †.
3. **Suda.** Russian: only about 100 entries by Maxim the Greek (16th c.). English: full (Suda On Line) (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Суда_(словарь)).
4. **Simplicius**, commentaries on Aristotle. Russian: only Physics I.1 excerpts (1998) and De caelo II excerpts (2005) (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Симпликий). English: Ancient Commentators on Aristotle (ACA) series, complete.
5. **Alexander of Aphrodisias**, commentaries (*Metaphysics*, *Prior Analytics*, *Topics*, *Meteorology*). Russian: none; only *De mixtione* (Солопова 2002) (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Александр_Афродисийский). English: ACA.
6. **Philoponus**, *Contra Proclum* and the Aristotle commentaries. Russian: only pp. 55–62 excerpts (Беневич 2009) (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Иоанн_Филопон). English: ACA.
7. **Syrianus**, *In Metaphysica*. Russian: none (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Сириан). English: ACA.
8. **Hermias**, *In Phaedrum*. Russian: none listed (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Гермий_Александрийский). English †.
9. **Olympiodorus**, commentaries on *Alcibiades*, *Gorgias*, *Phaedo*. Russian: none listed; only the *Life of Plato* (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Олимпиодор_Младший). English †.
10. **Proclus**, *In Euclidem I* and *In Alcibiadem*. Russian: none listed; *In Rempublicam* only partial (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Прокл_Диадох). English: Morrow; O'Neill †.
11. **Themistius**, *Orations*. Russian: 6 of 34 orations plus a short paraphrase excerpt (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Фемистий). English: Heather & Moncur; Penella †.

14. **Choricius.** Russian: excerpts only (see above). English: Penella †.
15. **Maximus of Tyre.** Russian: 3 of 41 *Dissertationes* (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Максим_Тирский). English: Trapp †.
16. **Dio Chrysostom.** Russian: about 16 of 80 orations (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Дион_Хрисостом). English: Loeb.

18. **Galen.** Russian: *De usu partium* (1971) plus about 5 volumes of *Сочинения* (2014–19), out of a corpus of about 400 works (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Гален). English: Cambridge and Loeb †.
19. **Paul of Aegina**, *Epitome*. Russian: none. English: Adams 1844–47, public domain (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Павел_Эгинский).

21. **Vettius Valens**, *Anthologies*. Russian: none (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Веттий_Валент). English †.
22. **Firmicus Maternus**, *Mathesis*. Russian: none listed (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Юлий_Фирмик_Матерн).
23. **Aelian**, *De natura animalium*. Russian: excerpts only (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Клавдий_Элиан). English: Loeb.

31. **Theodore of Mopsuestia**, commentaries. Russian: none listed (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Феодор_Мопсуестийский). English: Fathers of the Church series †.
32. **Servius.** Russian: *Aeneid* book 1 only (2001) (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Сервий).
33. **Priscian**, *Institutiones*. Russian: none (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Присциан).
34. **Apollonius Dyscolus.** Russian: none (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Аполлоний_Дискол). English: Householder †.
35. **Varro**, *De lingua Latina*. Russian: books VIII–X partial (1936) plus an excerpt (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Марк_Теренций_Варрон). English: Loeb.

39. **Ennodius.** Russian: none listed (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Магн_Феликс_Эннодий).
40. **Eustathius**, *Parekbolai* on Homer. Russian: none (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Евстафий_Солунский). **Tzetzes**, *Chiliades*: Russian excerpts only (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Иоанн_Цец).

**Avoid as "occupied" (active Russian work):** Proclus' *In Timaeum*, John Lydus, Aelius Aristides, Libanius' orations. Already complete: Corippus, Martianus, Claudian, *Panegyrici Latini*, Quintus.

**Alexander tradition:** Russian has Егунов's "История Александра Великого" (1960) and the 1965 *Александрия* volume. No Russian translation of Julius Valerius or the *Historia de preliis* was found, but this was not confirmed by search.

**Pilot picks** (high value, compact, public-domain text):
- Themistius' political orations
- Choricius
- Maximus of Tyre
- Oppian
- Selected chapters of Stobaeus
- Malalas books I–V (myth and Troy)

## 5. AI / machine translation discussion among Russian classicists
**Not verified.** The search budget ran out before this could be checked. Recommended: search eLibrary and CyberLeninka for «нейросеть / ChatGPT / машинный перевод + древнегреческий / латынь», plus Philologia Classica and Аристей tables of contents from 2023–26.

key_facts.fact: Stobaeus' Anthologium has never been fully translated into any modern language (ru.wiki states this explicitly); no Russian translation listed.
Russian Wikipedia notes scholia are usually not translated into modern languages; no Russian translations of scholia corpora are listed.
Choricius of Gaza: ru.wiki states that not a single complete translation of any of his works exists in Russian (only excerpts, 1968 and 2016).
Simplicius: only two Russian excerpts are listed (Physics I.1, 1998; De caelo II, 2005), while English ACA translations cover the commentaries.
Alexander of Aphrodisias: only De mixtione is translated into Russian (Солопова 2002); no Aristotle commentaries are listed.
Themistius: only 6 of 34 orations (3, 12, 25, 27, 30, 32) plus a De anima paraphrase excerpt exist in Russian.
Maximus of Tyre: only 3 of 41 Dissertationes are in Russian (II, V, XXXVI).
Photius' Bibliotheca exists in Russian only partially, about 100 codices (azbyka/Predanie edition).
Eusebius on azbyka: Praeparatio evangelica only book XI is in Russian; no Demonstratio evangelica is listed.
Russian translation of John Malalas exists only as excerpts (books II, V, VIII, XIV–XVIII) plus Istrin's Old Slavonic edition; no full modern Russian translation.
Proclus' Commentary on Timaeus is an active Russian project: book II serialized in ΣΧΟΛΗ 20.2 (2026) by S. Mesyats, RSF grant 25-18-00141; avoid as a gap.
ΣΧΟΛΗ is open access under a Creative Commons Attribution licence and indexed in Scopus, WoS, DOAJ and ERIH Plus, making it a natural partner journal.
Corippus' Iohannis received its first complete Russian (prose) translation in 2023 (Е.В. Старшова), and Martianus Capella a complete one in 2019 (Ю.А. Шахова), so they are no longer gaps.
Cassiodorus' Variae: only books I–II are available in Russian (С.В. Кулаев) on ancientrome.ru.
Galen in Russian: De usu partium (1971) plus about 5 volumes of Сочинения (2014–2019), a small fraction of roughly 400 works.

sweep:latin-scholia.corpus_overview:
About 26 Latin commentaries, grammarians and antiquarian texts were checked. Russian coverage is thin outside a few "big names". Nine texts already have full or near-full Russian translations, so they were dropped: Macrobius' Saturnalia (Zvirevich), Martianus Capella (Shakhov 2019), Isidore's Etymologiae (all 20 books on azbyka.ru), Censorinus (ВДИ 1986), Asconius (Khrustalev 2026), Fulgentius' Mitologiae (Guseinov/Mozhelyan/Bolgov, 1988–2016), Paul the Deacon's epitome of Festus (Pavlov 2012), Boethius' Porphyry commentary (1990) and De musica (2012), and Donatus' Ars minor (Petrova 1999).

Three have only partial Russian translations: Servius (excerpts on Aeneid 1, Fedorov 2001), Varro's De lingua Latina (excerpts from books VIII–X, 1936) and Priscian (minor works only).

No Russian translation was found for at least 18 others. These include the Terence commentary of Donatus, Tiberius Claudius Donatus, Porphyrio, ps.-Acro, the Juvenal and Persius scholia, the Lucan scholia, Lactantius Placidus, the Bobbio scholia, Festus' own text, Nonius, Terentianus, Calcidius, Boethius on the Categories, Grillius, Victorinus, Diomedes and Charisius.

English is also missing for about 12 of these. Festus is being translated (Fortson, ACLS 2026). Tiberius Claudius Donatus has only Book 1 in Italian (Pirovano 2025), described as the first translation into any modern language.

Two non-scholarly efforts overlap. Sourcelibrary.org posts AI-assisted CC BY-SA translations of public-domain scans, including Servius, Festus and Nonius, though Servius is not yet translated. A 2024 e-book offers a 'rough, unedited' English Servius. Neoscholia should set itself apart from both through its critical apparatus and visible review.

The search budget ran out partway through. The status of Priscian's Institutiones (English), Charisius, Diomedes, Victorinus and Pompeius was not fully checked, so they are left out of the candidate list.

candidates.title: Servius (+ Servius Danielis), Commentarii in Vergilii Aeneidem — Servius on the Aeneid; Сервий, «Комментарии к Энеиде». Proposed unit: commentary on Aeneid 6
candidates.author: Maurus Servius Honoratus; DServ additions largely from Aelius Donatus' lost commentary
candidates.size: Thilo–Hagen 3 vols (~1,900 pp., incl. Ecl./Georg.); est. 450k+ words. Aen. 6 est. 30–35k words (estimates)
candidates.edition: Thilo–Hagen, Leipzig 1878–1902 (public domain; scans on archive.org/sourcelibrary.org; Latin text on Perseus). Harvard Servius covers Aen. 1–5 only
candidates.ru_evidence: Only selected excerpts on Aen. 1, translated by N. A. Fedorov in «Энеида. С комментариями Сервия» (Лабиринт, 2001); ancientrome.ru/antlitr/servius/serv1.htm; ru.wikipedia lists nothing else
candidates.en_evidence: Book 4 only: McDonough, Prior & Stansbury (Bolchazy-Carducci 2002; BMCR 2005.03.16). An unedited 'rough' complete e-book (Authors of Mitologia.pt, 2024) is not scholarly
candidates.other_translations: No complete modern translation found (not verified for Italian/German partials)
candidates.value: The richest ancient Latin commentary: grammar, Roman religion and ritual, antiquarian lore, mythography, and fragments of lost authors (Varro, Cato). Aen. 6 covers eschatology, philosophy and ritual. Indispensable for Vergil scholars, historians of religion and Latinists
candidates.ai_feasibility: high — formulaic lemmatic prose. Risks: separating Servius from DServ layers, Greek quotations, textual variants
candidates.pilot_unit: Servius + DServ on Aen. 6 (est. 30–35k words); a first release could cover Aen. 6.1–263 (~10k words)

candidates.title: Aelius Donatus, Commentum Terenti — Commentary on Terence; Элий Донат, «Комментарий к Теренцию». Proposed unit: commentary on Adelphoe
candidates.author: Aelius Donatus (Jerome's teacher); surviving text is a later reassembly of excerpts
candidates.date: c. 350 CE; reassembled in late antiquity/early Middle Ages
candidates.size: Wessner, 2 vols (~1,000 pp.); est. 250k words; Heautontimorumenos commentary lost (estimate)
candidates.edition: Wessner, Teubner 1902–05 (public domain; Wessner d. 1933). Recent critical editions of the Andria and Eunuchus commentaries are copyrighted (BMCR 2018.02.10)
candidates.ru_evidence: Russian search found nothing; ru.wikipedia 'Элий Донат' lists only the Ars minor (Petrova 1999)
candidates.en_evidence: en.wikipedia: 'never been translated to English'; no translation found in searches
candidates.other_translations: Partial German translation (per en.wikipedia); no complete modern translation found
candidates.value: Main ancient source on Roman comic staging, delivery, gesture and character, on colloquial Latin and on Menander (Greek comparisons). Used by theatre historians, Latinists, Menander scholars, and students of Renaissance comic theory
candidates.ai_feasibility: medium-high — short lemmatic notes, but doublet notes from two recensions, lacunae and Greek quotations need flagging
candidates.pilot_unit: Commentary on Adelphoe (est. 35–45k words); a smaller pilot is the preface plus Adelphoe Act 1 (~8k words)

candidates.title: Pomponius Porphyrio, Commentum in Horatium Flaccum — Porphyrio's commentary on Horace; Порфирион, «Комментарий к Горацию». Proposed unit: on the Ars poetica
candidates.author: Pomponius Porphyrio
candidates.genre: School commentary on all of Horace
candidates.size: One volume (Meyer 1874; Holder 1894); est. 100–130k words (estimate)
candidates.edition: Meyer, Teubner 1874; Holder, Innsbruck 1894 (both public domain); Latin text in the Perseus catalogue
candidates.ru_evidence: ru.wikipedia 'Помпоний Порфирион' lists no translation; Russian search found none
candidates.en_evidence: No translation found. R. Pearse (blog, 2013) wishes the Horace scholia 'existed in English'
candidates.other_translations: None found (only studies, e.g. Formenti, MOM Éditions)
candidates.value: Oldest complete surviving Latin commentary on a poet: Horace's persons, realia, figures and metres. Preserves Neoptolemus of Parium's poetics (Ars poetica). Key for Horace studies, ancient literary criticism and the history of schooling
candidates.ai_feasibility: high — terse, clear prose; minor textual problems
candidates.pilot_unit: Commentary on the Ars poetica (est. 8–10k words); alternatively Odes Book 1

candidates.title: Tiberius Claudius Donatus, Interpretationes Vergilianae — Interpretations of Vergil; Тиберий Клавдий Донат, «Толкования Вергилия». Proposed unit: Book 4
candidates.author: Tiberius Claudius Donatus
candidates.genre: Rhetorical commentary on the whole Aeneid
candidates.size: 12 books; Georgii 2 vols (~1,300 pp.); est. 350–400k words; ~35–40k words per book (estimates)
candidates.edition: Georgii, Teubner 1905–06 (public domain). New critical edition of Book 1: Pirovano, Pàtron 2025 (copyright)
candidates.ru_evidence: No Russian translation found; no ru.wikipedia article; not in the ancientrome.ru catalogue
candidates.en_evidence: en.wikipedia lists none; the publisher calls Pirovano's Italian Book 1 (2025) 'the first in a modern language'
candidates.other_translations: Italian, Book 1 only (L. Pirovano, Bologna: Pàtron 2025)
candidates.value: The only complete late-antique rhetorical reading of the Aeneid, presenting it as praise of Aeneas. Important for ancient criticism, rhetoric and Vergil reception (55 editions printed 1488–1599). Untranslated beyond Book 1 in any language
candidates.ai_feasibility: high — fluent paraphrastic prose with few rare terms; the risk is verbosity, so the commentary should summarise rather than annotate line by line
candidates.pilot_unit: Book 4 (Dido), est. 35–40k words; can be cross-read against Servius on Book 4 in English

candidates.title: Scholia in Iuvenalem vetustiora — the old scholia on Juvenal; Древние схолии к Ювеналу. Proposed unit: scholia on Satires 1–6
candidates.author: Anonymous
candidates.size: Wessner 1931, c. 300 pp.; est. 60–80k words (estimate)
candidates.edition: Wessner, Teubner 1931 (Wessner d. 1933, so public domain in Russia/EU). Grazzini's edition of the later scholia (recentiora), 2011, is copyrighted
candidates.ru_evidence: No translation found; not in the ancientrome.ru catalogue
candidates.en_evidence: None found; BMCR 2012.03.42 mentions no translation; R. Pearse's blog offers only ad hoc passages
candidates.other_translations: None found
candidates.value: Preserves otherwise lost facts about Flavian Rome (Domitian's council in Sat. 4, incl. a fragment of Statius' De bello Germanico), prosopography, realia and Juvenal's vita. Valuable to social historians and scholars of satire
candidates.ai_feasibility: high — short notes; risk in corrupt names and lemmata
candidates.pilot_unit: Scholia on Satires 1–6 (est. 25–30k words), or Satires 4 + 6 (est. 12–15k words)

candidates.title: Sextus Pompeius Festus, De verborum significatu (surviving Codex Farnesianus, M–V) — On the Meaning of Words; Фест, «О значении слов». Proposed unit: letter M
candidates.author: Sextus Pompeius Festus (epitomising Verrius Flaccus)
candidates.size: c. 3,300 entries overall; Lindsay 1913 c. 520 pp. incl. Paulus; Festus' own text est. 50–60k words (estimate)

candidates.ru_evidence: Only Paul the Deacon's epitome: A. A. Pavlov (Сыктывкар 2012, 300 pp.; selections in ВДИ 2012 №2), per ru.wikipedia. No Russian translation of Festus' own text found

candidates.title: Varro, De lingua Latina, Books V–VII — On the Latin Language; Варрон, «О латинском языке» (RU-gap)
candidates.author: M. Terentius Varro
candidates.size: Books V–VII est. 25–30k words (Books V–X survive; estimate)

candidates.title: Lactantius Placidus, Commentum in Statii Thebaida — Commentary on Statius' Thebaid; Лактанций Плацид, «Комментарий к Фиваиде». Proposed unit: Thebaid 1

candidates.title: Boethius, In Categorias Aristotelis libri IV — Commentary on Aristotle's Categories; Боэций, «Комментарий к Категориям Аристотеля». Proposed unit: Book I

candidates.edition: Migne PL 64 (public domain); no modern critical edition found
